full_text:
Mohammed, Sultan of Cairo, was a brave warrior but cursed with a fiery, impulsive temper. Whenever angered, he issued hasty decrees of execution that he later regretted in bitter remorse.

Realizing his dangerous weakness, he summoned his venerable Grand Vizier, Burhan al-Din, and said:
'O wise counselor, my temper is like a desert whirlwind. I appoint thee the guardian of my soul. Whenever thou seest me inflamed with wrath and ready to order a man's death, thou hast my royal permission to delay the decree three days, presenting me three questions before the blade is drawn.'

Weeks later, a foreign ambassador brought a rare gift: a luminous crystal vase of ancient Persian manufacture, translucent as morning air and engraved with floral traceries. The Sultan prized it above all treasures in his citadel.

One afternoon, a young cupbearer accidentally tripped on the edge of the royal carpet. The crystal vase slipped from his hands and shattered into a thousand glittering shards upon the marble floor.

Furious, the Sultan leaped to his feet, drew his scimitar, and shouted: 'Behead him this instant!'

Vizier Burhan al-Din stepped forward, bowed low, and placed his hand gently upon the executioner's scimitar:
'Remember thy covenant, O King. Grant the three days.'

The Sultan, trembling with rage, consented.

On the third morning, when the Sultan's anger had subsided into calm reflection, Burhan al-Din brought the cupbearer before the throne and asked the three questions:
'First: Can the execution of this youth reassemble the shattered crystal?'
The Sultan answered softly: 'No.'
'Second: Does the loss of an earthen, fragile object equal the destruction of a living human soul created by Allah?'
The Sultan replied with bowed head: 'No.'
'Third: Which memory will bring greater peace to thy heart when thou facest the Eternal Judge—the memory of a broken vase avenged with blood, or the memory of royal mercy extended to a trembling servant?'

Tears filled Sultan Mohammed's eyes. He sheathed his sword, embraced his wise Vizier, and rewarded the cupbearer with freedom and gold. From that day forward, the Sultan became celebrated throughout Egypt as Mohammed the Just, proving that true sovereignty lies in the mastery of oneself.
moral: A ruler's greatest victory is overcoming his own wrath and governing through mercy and steadfast counsel. [ZH]
